newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia declares war on pesky rabbits.
newsitem.headline: Australia declares war on pesky rabbits.

text.p: Australia has declared biological war on an estimated 200 million rabbits.

The rabbit population received its first exposure to the deadly calicivirus disease near the outback town of Wagga Wagga, where New South Wales Agriculture Minister Richard Amery released 20 infected rabbits into the wild.
Farmers blame the creatures -- imported by a British hunting buff in the 19th century -- with causing extensive damage to crops and driving indigenous animals and plants to the verge of extinction.
"It's probably the best news the environment has had in 20 years," said Mick Keogh, a farmers' representative.
Government officials say the virus will eventually be released at 280 sites in all of Australia's states and territories, although some wild rabbits have already been accidentally infected.

Calicivirus kills most rabbits in 12 to 24 hours by causing massive internal bleeding. The virus was first detected in Europe in 1984, traced to a train shipment of angora rabbits from China. The virus swept through Europe's rabbit population, prompting scientists to harness it for pest control purposes.
Scientists say the virus has been modified to infect only rabbits and that humans are not susceptible to it.
Supporters of the virus' release hope the disease will eradicate up to 80 percent of the rabbit population within two years. Rabbits currently outnumber humans in Australia by around 10 to one.
Amery said rabbits were responsible for the decline of many native Australian animals such as the wombat and the bandicoot-like bilby, as well as native plants pushed to extinction,
Others criticised the move as premature, however, saying the virus could harm other animals.

"We question the assurances of scientists and regulators that the virus will not infect native or domestic animals and cannot cross into humans," Bob Phelps, a spokesman for the Australian Conservation Foundation, said.
"The virus crossed into rabbits and it may only be a matter of time before it moves on," he said.

Dr Lyn Hinds of Australia's Vertebrate Biocontrol Centre, which is involved in government pest control activities, said she could not rule out the disease spreading to humans and other animals but the odds were against it.
"No one can categorically say that it will never jump over into another species, but the evidence to date shows that it seems to be highly specific to the rabbit," Hinds said.

Australia is also battling to reduce its population of kangaroos, estimated to be in the millions, Hinds said. One long-term project under consideration was to use anti-fertility drugs to control the country's most famous native creature.
